gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1017t:
Veterans Affairs, GAO-05-1017T of September 14, 2005, centers on one job: the chief information officer at the Department of Veterans Affairs. VA leans hard on computers to serve veterans and their kin. It sought about $2.1 billion for that work in fiscal year 2006. The Clinger-Cohen Act of 1996 made the CIO the focal point for tech choices in each agency.

GAO traces how the CIO role grew across the federal government. It then gives the past record of the post at VA. The point is stark: with no strong CIO at the hub, a vast tech budget drifts. Past GAO work at VA and peer agencies backs the claim.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1027t:
Wrong rent aid sums sit at the core of GAO-05-1027T, a statement of September 27, 2005, on the Department of Housing and Urban Development. In fiscal year 2003, HUD paid about $28 billion to help some 5 million low-income tenants. Aid flows through vouchers, public housing, and project-based Section 8 deals. Each year, some sums come out too high or too low.

HUD built a fix-it project to find the size and causes of those errors. GAO sums up what that work showed, based on a February 2005 report. It lists the main error sources and the steps HUD took to cut them down.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1037t:
Capitol Visitor Center, GAO-05-1037T of September 15, 2005, gives the Senate a fresh check on a big build that kept slipping. The Architect of the Capitol runs the project. GAO tracks its timetable, its cost, and its cash since a July 14, 2005 hearing on the same build. Contractors had just pushed dates back again in August.

GAO held off on firm end dates this time. The Architect had not yet judged the new timetable, and called the added time too long. Cost sums tied to the old dates could not be trusted yet. The statement lays out the risk points and what must settle before firm sums return.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1047t:
Energy Markets: Gasoline Price Trends, GAO-05-1047T of September 21, 2005, was given to a Senate panel as pump prices spiked in the wake of Hurricane Katrina. Prices in hit zones rose over $3.00 per gallon. One case hit almost $6.00 per gallon. Some stations ran dry. Cheap fuel had long fed U.S. growth, so a long spike posed a real threat.

The statement breaks down how pump prices get set. Crude oil costs, refining, and transport each take a share. It then names the forces apt to move prices next. No single cause runs the chart, the text shows; supply shocks just hit fast.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-307t:
Coast Guard, GAO-05-307T of April 20, 2005, gives early notes on a fleet that wears out as its swap lags. In 2002, the Coast Guard began a swap and upgrade plan worth $19 billion to $24 billion. It covers cutters and planes that work far off shore. The old fleet breaks down at a pace that cannot hold, the Guard warns.

GAO tracks how the old fleet's shape changed from fiscal year 2000 through 2004. It lists what the Guard does to keep the old hulls at work. It names the strain a faster swap would place on the buyers. Past and fresh GAO work both feed the notes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-347t:
Indian Issues, GAO-05-347T of February 10, 2005, gives the pace of a long queue: groups that seek to be known as tribes. The Bureau of Indian Affairs set the proof path in 1978. A group must show it has lived as a tribe since old times. Critics call the calls uneven and the waits vast. Lawmakers have fought the point for over 27 years.

GAO rests on its November 2, 2001 report for the base tale. It tells how slow the path ran then. It lists what the federal ack office has done since to speed it. Pace has grown, the title grants; the queue will still take years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-357t:
Transportation Security, GAO-05-357T of February 15, 2005, argues that the guard of U.S. travel ways needs one plan, not many hunches. Travel nets cross the land and reach past its shores. They move millions of folks and tons of goods each day. That flow makes them rich marks for terror, and hard to seal. A guard that slows flow too much harms the land it guards.

The Transportation Security Administration must spread thin cash where risk runs most high. GAO tells how it and its parent arm weigh risk across air and land modes. It tells how checks, passes, and tech work could join for gain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-447t:
GAO's own funding request for fiscal year 2006 is presented in testimony GAO-05-447T, dated May 23, 2005. The statement thanks Congress for past support and makes the case for the year ahead. It frames GAO as a source of fact-based, nonpartisan work for Congress. It also points to the nation's budget deficit and long-term fiscal imbalance as reasons that oversight would matter more, not less.

The testimony cites GAO's recent report on the challenges of the 21st century. That report urged a fresh look at what the federal government should do and how it should pay for it. GAO argued that money spent on its work brings a sound return for Congress and the public. The statement is useful as a record of how the agency described its role and needs at that time. It pairs the budget ask with a wider warning on federal finances.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-517t:
Draft rules for the Pentagon's new personnel system draw further comment in testimony GAO-05-517T, presented on April 12, 2005. The National Security Personnel System would reshape how the Defense Department manages more than 700,000 civilian staff. The rules were released for public comment on February 14, 2005. The comment period closed on March 16, 2005. Talks with employee groups were set to follow.

Many ideas in the draft match proven practice, GAO said. Pay bands and pay tied to performance are among them. So is giving performance more weight when jobs are cut. GAO's worries ran in three lines. The rules leave the system's inner workings undefined, with no clear guards against unfair use. They do not require core competencies that tell staff what good work means. They set no path for staff to stay part of planning and rollout. Ten unions had sued over their role in shaping the labor side of the plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-527t:
The tax gap, and what closing it would take, is the subject of testimony GAO-05-527T, given on April 14, 2005. The Internal Revenue Service put the gap for tax year 2001 at $312 billion to $353 billion. After late payments and enforcement, the net gap falls to $257 billion to $298 billion. The gap comes from income hidden on returns, taxes owed but unpaid, and returns never filed.

On current paths, the federal deficit grows beyond what growth alone can fix. A basic rethink of spending and tax policy will be needed. Collecting more of what is owed would help, GAO said. But compliance has not improved, and may have worsened. Enforcement staff and audits had begun to recover after years of decline. GAO argued the gap must be attacked on many fronts at once. Simpler tax law, better service, and stronger enforcement all have a part.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-567t:
Homeland Security's handling of the federal computer security law is reviewed in testimony GAO-05-567T, given on April 14, 2005. The department is the third largest in the federal government. It runs many major systems for both operations and office work. The 2002 law, FISMA, requires yearly reports on security duties. GAO drew on the department's own fiscal year 2004 report and on its inspector general's findings.

Most of the tracked measures moved up in 2004. The share of staff and contractors who had security awareness training jumped from 14 percent in fiscal year 2003 to 85 percent in fiscal year 2004. More systems had been reviewed as well. But the department still falls short on most legal duties, GAO said. It lacks a complete and exact list of its own systems. Its process for fixing known flaws does not work well.  The testimony shows a young department improving on paper while basic controls lag.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-627t:
Wildland fire strategy, structure protection, and radio links share this testimony, GAO-05-627T of April 26, 2005. It draws on two GAO studies from early 2005. Fires grow fiercer as brush builds up and homes spread into fire country. Crews from many agencies often cannot talk by radio because their sets clash. Progress on a joint fire plan is real but unfinished.

The testimony lists ways to harden homes, from cleared yards to fire-safe roofs, and tech paths to shared speech on the fire line. GAO had urged the farm and interior departments to finish a joint strategy with costs; both agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-657t:
The Airport and Airway Trust Fund's shrinking cushion is charted in GAO-05-657T, testimony dated May 4, 2005. Ticket, fuel, and cargo taxes feed the fund that pays for airport grants and air traffic gear. Its free balance topped $7 billion in 1991 and 1999, then slid from $7.3 billion in 2001 by about $1 billion a year, to near $2 billion at the end of 2004.

Forecasts show the fund covering planned spending for 3 years if traffic and fares match hopes. A 5 percent revenue miss shrinks the cushion sharply. A 10 percent miss empties it by 2006 or 2007. The taxes lapse in 2007.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-707t:
Tax agency progress and strain share GAO testimony GAO-05-707T, dated May 19, 2005. Since the 1998 reform law, phone access, answer accuracy, and web services have all improved markedly. Enforcement staffing fell after 1998 and has only lately turned up. Chasing unpaid tax stays a high-risk field. The systems rebuild has gained controls and hardware but remains prone to delay and overrun, as its history warns.

Next gains hinge on scarce resources. GAO floats long-term goals, user fees, private debt collectors, and help from states and volunteers as ways to stretch the budget.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-827t:
Cybersecurity for key systems is surveyed in testimony GAO-05-827T, presented July 19, 2005. Linked computers now run much of national life. That same linkage puts key operations at risk. Law and policy made Homeland Security the hub for guarding these systems. GAO summed up its past work. It covered the department's duties, its progress, its challenges, and GAO's past advice.

GAO found the department holds 13 key duties in this field. It has not fully met any of them. A cyber division and a readiness team were set up. Forums now build trust among officials. But no national threat and weakness assessments exist yet. No joint recovery plans for key Internet functions exist either. GAO named blocks: an unsettled structure, low awareness, and weak sharing with partners.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-847t:
Design choices for personal retirement accounts fill testimony GAO-05-847T, delivered June 23, 2005. Social Security faces long-term money strain as the population ages. Some reform plans would add individual accounts. A House panel asked GAO to walk through the design issues. The choices span three phases: putting money in, growing it, and paying it out.

GAO urged that any reform be weighed as a full package. Accounts touch retirement, disability, and survivor parts of the system at once. In the first phase, lawmakers must set the payment rate and decide if taking part is a choice. In the growth phase, they must set who invests and how much choice savers get. In the payout phase, they must shape how savings turn into income. Each choice shifts cost and complexity, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-857t:
Zero down payment mortgages and risk fill testimony GAO-05-857T, delivered June 30, 2005. Congress weighed a pilot to insure home loans with no down payment. The Federal Housing Administration would run it. The risks of such a product are not well understood. GAO drew on its February 2005 report on new loan products. It shared how lenders design and guard low down payment loans.

GAO found two factors matter most in judging a loan's risk. They are the loan-to-value ratio and the borrower's credit score. Higher ratios and lower scores mean riskier loans. Other lenders add guards for new products: extra insurance cover, stricter checks, and caps on volume. The housing agency can require extra cover but does not use that power now. It told GAO it would likely not set a credit score floor for the new product.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-907t:
Improper payments across government are reported in testimony GAO-05-907T, given July 20, 2005. A 2002 law made agencies hunt, estimate, and report such payments. Fiscal year 2004 was the first year of full reporting under the law. The testimony sums up work GAO reported in March 2005. It covers progress and the gaps that remain.

GAO found agencies have largely taken up the task. The budget office keeps strong pressure on through its management agenda. But some agencies had not yet assessed risk for all programs or built estimates. So the true size of the problem stays unknown. In the 29 agency reports GAO reviewed, 17 agencies reported over $45 billion in improper payments across 41 programs. That is about $10 billion more than the year before, mostly due to changed methods.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-937t:
Used electronics and recycling get early findings in testimony GAO-05-937T, presented July 26, 2005. Millions of computers go obsolete each year. Only a fraction are recycled. Old gear can leak toxic lead. It also holds precious metals that cost much energy and land to mine. GAO summed up what is known about volumes and harms. It weighed what shapes recycling and reuse.

Some data suggest over 100 million computers, monitors, and TVs go obsolete each year. Most used gear is likely stored in basements, garages, and warehouses. Stored units may later be recycled, dumped, or shipped abroad. Metals like copper, gold, and aluminum are lost when gear is landfilled. Cost blocks wider recycling, GAO found. People must pay fees and haul gear to drop-off points. A full report was to follow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1087t:
In testimony dated September 13, 2006, GAO said the Department of Homeland Security had yet to lead well on cybersecurity. Federal law made DHS the focal point for guarding systems behind key national infrastructure. GAO summed up recent reports on DHS duties, hurdles, and fixes. One duty stands out: planning how the Internet would recover after a major disruption.

In 2005 GAO found DHS had begun work on 13 key duties but fully met none. By 2006 it had made progress, yet none was fully done. Its Internet recovery work lacked clear time frames. Trust was a core problem, and a top cyber post sat empty over a year. GAO pointed to about 25 past recommendations as a road map. They call for threat assessments, warning tools, and stronger teamwork.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1107t:
Electric lines crossing Alaska Native allotments are the dispute at the heart of GAO-06-1107T, testimony from September 2006. The 1906 allotment law let individual Alaska Natives claim homesteads of up to 160 acres. Copper Valley Electric Association holds rights-of-way inside some allotments, and some owners call the lines a trespass. The testimony rests on GAO's 2004 report on the conflict.

GAO counted 14 cases where the rights-of-way were in dispute. The clashes grew from land claims that predate the lines, from state grants the Interior Department does not accept, and from lines built with no grant at all. Existing remedies had settled few cases. Copper Valley could bargain with owners, move its lines, or use condemnation. It viewed each path as costly or harmful to community ties. GAO laid out four legislative options for Congress, including a change to the date rule that drives many disputes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1127t:
NASA's Crew Exploration Vehicle and the risks around it are addressed in GAO-06-1127T, testimony from September 2006. NASA plans to spend nearly $230 billion over two decades on the Vision for Space Exploration. The vehicle is one of the vision's largest projects. In July 2006 GAO questioned whether the full program was affordable. It also faulted NASA's buying approach for the vehicle. This statement adds a review of NASA's wider acquisition rules.

GAO's core concern is knowledge. NASA lets projects advance without proof that key technologies are mature or designs are stable. That pattern invites cost growth and delay. GAO urged NASA to set knowledge tests at each major gate in its new engineering policy. Projects would show mature technology before build approval and a stable design before fabrication. The testimony warns that sound management, not hope, decides whether the exploration plan holds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-207t:
Lessons from private disability insurers for the veterans agency fill GAO-06-207T, testimony presented on October 27, 2005. The Department of Veterans Affairs pays some veterans at the full disability rate when service injuries leave them unable to work. Awards under this Individual Unemployability benefit have grown fast in five years. GAO compared the agency's checks with the habits of three private insurers it studied in 2001.

The insurers build return-to-work thinking into each claim from the start. They press claimants toward treatment and work trials, and they pay bosses to offer jobs. They match staff skills to the goal of getting people back to work. The veterans agency lags on each point. Its review lacks a work specialist to judge what a veteran could still do. Its process centers on what veterans cannot do, and it offers few paths back to a job.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-227t:
Final rules for a new Pentagon personnel system are weighed in GAO-06-227T, testimony presented on November 17, 2005. Congress gave the Defense Department wide freedom in November 2003 to design a modern staff system. The National Security Personnel System rules came out in final form on November 1, 2005. They bring pay bands and pay for performance. GAO commented on the draft rules months earlier. This statement gives its view of the final text.

The final rules hold many sound principles, GAO said. They promise a market-based, performance-driven pay system. In layoff choices, strong performers gain an edge. Workers' representatives get a voice as the system rolls out. Yet key details stay unwritten, from how goals link to mission to how fairness gets checked. Core skills are allowed, not required. GAO urged a full communications plan and the groundwork to run the system well.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-257t:
The case for changing how the Pentagon buys weapons is made in GAO-06-257T, testimony presented on November 15, 2005. The Defense Department steers a weapon portfolio worth about $1.3 trillion. Its buying has sat on GAO's high-risk list since 1990. Cost overruns, missed deadlines, and weak results repeat across programs. Hundreds of GAO reports have named the causes and the cures. Congress asked GAO to pull that record together: what is wrong, and what do the winners do right.

Business as usual carries the risk, GAO argued. Strong programs start with a sound business case and mature technology. They hold managers to account for results they can control. Weak ones launch on hope and pay for it for decades. With the budget under strain, the waste is hard to defend. The testimony is a brief for reform drawn from 15 years of case evidence.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-297t:
Charities in disaster relief, and the lessons of past storms, shape GAO-06-297T, testimony delivered December 13, 2005. Hurricanes Katrina and Rita wrecked lives across Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Texas. Doubts rose about how well charities and government can answer such ruin. The National Response Plan names charities as partners with set duties. After the storms they gave both quick relief and long-term help beside federal agencies. GAO gathered what earlier disasters taught about charity work. It added early observations from the Gulf Coast response.

Knowing what went right and wrong is the first step to a stronger response, GAO argued. Charities bring local roots, volunteers, and trust that agencies lack. They also vary widely in capacity and reach. The testimony feeds GAO's ongoing study of the federal and charitable effort. It frames goodwill as a resource that still needs planning. Future storms will test whether the lessons were learned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-357t:
More service members would soon leave duty, and veterans needed jobs. In testimony GAO-06-357T (February 2, 2006), GAO sums up GAO work on the Veterans' Employment and Training Service. Labor expected the number leaving active duty to rise by 200,000 a year. The Jobs for Veterans Act of 2002 reshaped two Labor programs for veterans.

One program serves disabled veterans who need outreach. The other links veterans with employers. GAO checked new staff roles, incentive awards, and performance measures. It asked whether results for veterans had improved. It also studied weak points in oversight. The testimony calls for greater accountability and other Labor action.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-417t:
The watchdog asked Congress for its own yearly funding in this statement. Delivered March 10, 2006, testimony GAO-06-417T presents GAO's fiscal year 2007 budget request. GAO asked for budget authority of $509.4 million. That is a 5 percent rise over its revised fiscal year 2006 level. The request supports a staffing level of 3,267 full-time equivalents. That level is 50 more than planned for fiscal year 2006.

GAO says tighter budgets shaped the request. The funds would aid gains in productivity and technology. They would help rebuild staff for work on disaster aid, terrorism, homeland security, forensic auditing, and health care. Readers get the agency's case for its funds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-467t:
Major emergencies test whether agencies and responders can truly work as one. Testimony GAO-06-467T, given February 23, 2006, discusses emergency preparedness and response. Sound response needs joint planning across responder types, places, and levels of government. September 11, 2001 changed the context for federal involvement. Hurricane Katrina raised fresh questions about readiness for catastrophic events.

GAO calls cooperation the biggest challenge in preparedness. It covers joint planning, exercises, and capability checks. It notes how little is known about how states and local areas finance this work. It also reviews federal policy tools, such as a uniform incident command structure. Readers get issues and challenges, stated plainly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-477t:
Federal forms eat billions of hours a year, and a law aims to keep that load in check. On March 8, 2006, testimony GAO-06-477T reviewed the Paperwork Reduction Act. The act seeks to cut the burden of federal information collections. It also seeks to raise their public benefit. The Office of Management and Budget must approve all such collections. Agency chief information officers must review them first.

GAO draws on past work and an expert forum held in February 2005. It studied a government-wide sample of collections and work at four agencies. New approaches can strengthen collection and reduce burden, GAO said. Readers get case studies of 12 approved collections.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-487t:
Two fighter programs worth almost $320 billion anchor this update. Testimony GAO-06-487T, dated March 16, 2006, covers the F-22A and Joint Strike Fighter programs. Both aim to replace aging tactical fighters. Many of those aircraft have served over 20 years. Past GAO work found poor results in major weapon buys. Cost and schedule overruns cut buying power and delayed new capability.

A House panel asked for updated testimony. GAO judges whether the two business cases can be carried out. It reports the status of the wider renewal effort. It also sets out options for renewing the air forces. The goals are not backed by knowledge-based cases, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-497t:
Some federal programs are so prone to waste that GAO keeps a standing risk list. Testimony GAO-06-497T, dated March 15, 2006, explains GAO's High-Risk Program. Since 1990, GAO has reported a high-risk list to each new Congress. The most recent update came in January 2005. It gave the 109th Congress the status of old and new risk areas. High-risk areas face fraud, waste, abuse, and mismanagement.

GAO now also flags areas needing broad change for economy and effectiveness. Lasting fixes could save billions, the statement says. They could also improve service and public trust. Readers get the logic of the list and why it persists between Congresses.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-527t:
Weak computer security across government has been a high-risk problem since 1997. GAO's GAO-06-527T testimony, delivered March 16, 2006, tracks agency progress under a 2002 security law. The Federal Information Security Management Act strengthened the federal security program. It set evaluation and reporting duties for agencies. GAO most recently listed information security as high risk in January 2005. Attacks on commercial systems added to the concern.

GAO sums up progress and challenges as reported by the budget office, agencies, and inspectors general. Agencies show mixed progress, it said. The testimony names actions needed to improve reporting. It also addresses the root weaknesses behind the scores.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-557t:
Bombings in London showed how open rail systems are to attack. On March 29, 2006, testimony GAO-06-557T reviewed passenger rail security. It rests mainly on a September 2005 GAO report. The July 2005 London subway attacks killed and injured many riders. They focused new attention on rail security worldwide. GAO contacted 32 U.S. rail operators for that report. It also contacted 13 operators in seven European and Asian countries.

GAO presents security practices used at home and abroad. It reviews federal funding for rail security and the use of risk in funding choices. It tracks steps to improve coordination between two departments. Judging foreign practice and risk can guide U.S. efforts, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-587t:
A bigger fleet built with smaller crews is the Navy's long-range bet. Testimony GAO-06-587T, given March 30, 2006, examines the Navy's long-range shipbuilding plans. The plan develops many new ship classes with advanced technology. Ships would use reduced crews and more automation to lower costs. The fleet would grow by about 10 percent. It would average about 309 ships through 2036. The effort will cost billions of dollars.

A House armed services panel asked GAO to examine the plan. GAO discusses the many objectives the plan must meet. It names challenges in carrying it out. It also suggests ways to ease the tension between demand for ships and supply of funds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-597t:
Running a federal screening workforce is a management task as much as a security one. Testimony GAO-06-597T, given April 4, 2006, reviews the Transportation Security Administration's workforce and airport security. The agency had run passenger and baggage screening for over three years. GAO focuses on progress in strengthening aviation security. It also keeps the challenges in view. Federal security directors and screening officers hold operational duty for passengers and bags.

GAO reports progress and problems in managing that federal workforce. It reviews agency actions on wider airport security oversight. Progress has been made, GAO said. Challenges remain in both areas. Readers get workforce and oversight findings in one statement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-657t:
Pay debts owed by wounded soldiers are the focus of GAO-06-657T, testimony dated April 27, 2006. Many Army National Guard and Reserve soldiers who served in the Global War on Terrorism faced pay and travel payment errors. For hundreds of sick and injured soldiers, those errors turned into debts the Army said they owed. The debts brought real hardship to soldiers who were already recovering from wounds.

GAO told Congress that weak, complex pay systems caused many of the errors. Soldiers often learned of debts late and struggled to dispute them. GAO drew on its earlier reports and testimony on military pay problems since September 11, 2001. The testimony presses the Army to fix the systems and treat injured soldiers fairly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-697t:
Rebuilding Iraq after the fall of its former regime is surveyed in GAO-06-697T, testimony dated April 25, 2006. The United States, coalition partners, and global bodies faced a costly effort to stabilize and rebuild the nation. The work went on amid an unstable security setting. At the same time, Iraqis were moving toward their first permanent government. GAO summed up progress and open challenges in governance, security, rebuilding, and financing.

GAO found that Iraq had made some progress on political, security, and economic fronts. Iraqis had taken a growing part in the political process, and Iraqi forces were expanding. Yet violence, weak institutions, and funding strains slowed the effort. The testimony gives lawmakers a compact status report on a vast overseas undertaking.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-707t:
Explaining the United States to the world is assessed in GAO-06-707T, testimony GAO gave on May 3, 2006. Polls showed continued negative views of the United States in the Muslim world. Public diplomacy, led by the State Department, aims to explain policy, counter false claims, and build mutual understanding. Since 2003, GAO had issued three reports on these efforts. This testimony sums up the state of the work.

GAO said public diplomacy resources had shifted toward the Muslim world. But strategy, planning, and coordination efforts remained inadequate. The efforts lacked certain basic communication elements, such as clear target audiences and feedback. The government also lacked a true interagency strategy for the task. GAO warned that these persistent challenges limited results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-747t:
Security clearances for contractor staff are the focus of GAO-06-747T, testimony presented on May 17, 2006. The Defense Department handles about 2 million active personnel security clearances. About one-third cover industry workers on contracts for the department and over 20 other agencies. Slow eligibility decisions raise the risk of leaks and drive up contract costs. GAO updated Congress on why industry clearances lag.

GAO pointed to an unexpected surge in clearance requests and to funding constraints that slowed processing. Investigators and adjudicators could not keep pace with demand. GAO warned that these impediments could continue if left unaddressed. Other risks loomed too, such as rising demand for high-level clearances. The testimony shows how a paperwork backlog becomes a security and cost problem.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-777t:
Privacy duties across federal agencies are surveyed in GAO-06-777T, testimony GAO gave on May 17, 2006. New technology makes it ever easier for the government to gather and process personal information. Two laws anchor privacy duties: the Privacy Act and the E-Government Act of 2002. They require agencies to protect data and tell the public how it is used. GAO summed up the key challenges agencies face in meeting those duties.

GAO noted that many agencies had named officials to lead privacy work. Some had created chief privacy officers, and these roles were gaining prominence. New laws and guidance pushed agencies to give one senior official agencywide charge of privacy. Even so, agencies struggled to apply old rules to new data practices. The testimony frames privacy as a management duty, not just a legal one.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-787t:
State child welfare spending is the topic of GAO-06-787T, testimony GAO presented on May 23, 2006. For fiscal year 2004, state and local staff judged an estimated 872,000 children to be victims of abuse or neglect. Title IV-B of the Social Security Act funds a wide range of services for these families. GAO described how states used the two parts of the program. GAO also judged what federal oversight of state activity could teach.

GAO found that states used the first part mainly to staff and run child welfare programs and serve foster care families. The second part went mainly to prevention and support for families at risk. The line between service types, though, was hard to draw clearly. GAO said stronger federal oversight could show where action is needed. Better facts would help improve services and legal compliance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-827t:
Another monthly check on the Capitol Visitor Center appears in GAO-06-827T, testimony GAO gave on June 28, 2006. GAO tracked the Architect of the Capitol's progress on milestones and the project schedule. The update covers the period since the hearing of May 24, 2006. It also flags key challenges and risks that still face the underground visitor project. GAO had warned for months that the opening dates were too tight.

This time, the schedule itself moved. GAO reported that the architect had extended the project's completion and opening dates. Construction kept advancing, but serious problems drove the delay. Trouble centered on the fire protection system, the gift shops, and the utility tunnel. The testimony records a project conceding, at last, that its dates could not hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-877t:
Weak oversight and buying flaws at the United Nations could hurt its planned headquarters renovation, priced by the UN at about $1.6 billion. GAO gave this testimony, GAO-06-877T, on June 20, 2006. It drew on recent GAO work on the UN Office of Internal Oversight Services, known as OIOS, and on UN buying rules.

GAO checked whether OIOS funding kept it free from outside pressure. It also checked OIOS work against world audit norms and UN buying against control norms. GAO urged U.S. officials to back budget freedom for OIOS, closer fit with those norms, and fixes to UN buying. Readers get a clear map of the weak points found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-897t:
A data breach at the Department of Veterans Affairs, exposing personal data on millions of veterans, frames GAO testimony GAO-06-897T, dated June 20, 2006. Strong federal security programs guard personal data and privacy. Weak ones leave both at risk.

GAO spoke on the department's security program and its known weak points. It set out ways agencies can stop improper release of personal data. It also took up how and when to tell people of a privacy breach. The testimony draws on past GAO reports and expert views given to Congress. It remains a plain guide to federal data care duties.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-957t:
Purchase card abuse at the Department of Homeland Security is exposed in GAO testimony GAO-06-957T, dated July 19, 2006. After the 2005 Gulf hurricanes, department staff made thousands of card buys for rescue and relief work. GAO and the department's inspector general probed that spending together.

They tested a sample of buys and mined all card data for five months from June 2005. GAO asked if card controls worked, and if key checks gave fair proof of proper use. Signs of fraud and misuse were there. Weak controls, the title states, left the department highly open to bad card use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-977t:
Gene-based diet tests sold on the web mislead buyers, GAO states in testimony GAO-06-977T, dated July 27, 2006. Firms claim a cheek swab can guide diet and exercise to fit a person's genes. Buyers mail in their own samples and get tailored advice back.

GAO bought tests from four web sites. It sent 12 samples from one woman and 2 from an unrelated man. It dressed them up as 14 varied adults, with mixed ages, weights, and habits. Experts in genes and food aided the probe. The results showed claims that did not hold up. The testimony is a sharp case study in direct-to-buyer health sales.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-997t:
State watch over rail transit safety is described in GAO testimony GAO-06-997T, dated July 19, 2006. Rail transit moves millions of people each day. Unlike most travel modes, state bodies named for the task hold safety and security watch, under Federal Transit Administration rules.

GAO told how that state program is built. It set out what is known of its effect on rail safety and security. It named the hurdles the program faces. It also covered systems that cross state lines. The work drew on a poll of state and transit bodies, and talks with 24 of 25 watch agencies. Findings here are early, from work in progress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1047t:
Drawing foreign students to U.S. universities is the concern in GAO testimony GAO-07-1047T, dated June 29, 2007. More foreign students study in the United States than in any other land. They earn one-third or more of U.S. master's and doctor's degrees in several science and tech fields.

Yet entry had dipped, and post-2001 policy shifts raised fears for the flow. GAO drew on past and current work, plus a September 2006 forum of experts. It set out hurdles in drawing such students. It weighed what a weaker flow means for U.S. rivalry in the world. Students who go home, it notes, also aid U.S. public outreach.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1097t:
Foster youth on the edge of adult life are the focus of GAO testimony GAO-07-1097T, dated July 12, 2007. The Foster Care Independence Act of 1999 doubled yearly federal funds for such programs, to $140 million. The aim is to ready youth in care for life on their own.

GAO told how states split those funds. It set out services given, and hurdles that stay. It weighed how states join up programs to deliver aid. It tracked headway by states and the Health and Human Services arm toward program proof duties. The base is a 2004 GAO report, with fresh facts from 2007 work. Federal steps would help states, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1107t:
Iraq's oil sector resists repair, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1107T, dated July 18, 2007. Oil is key to Iraq's economy. Export income makes over half of its gross domestic product, and over 90 percent of government income. A sound oil law is part of the same build.

GAO set out U.S. aims for the oil sector, and headway toward them. It named the chief hurdles U.S. staff face in helping Iraq restore that sector. It traced work to pass and use a hydrocarbon law. The statement rests on a May 2007 GAO report, with data updated where apt. Grave hurdles impair the work, the title states.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1137t:
Farm payments to the dead are the topic of GAO testimony GAO-07-1137T, dated July 24, 2007. Farmers get about $20 billion a year in federal farm payments. Estates can take payments for the first 2 years after a death. For later years, the Department of Agriculture must find the estate is not held open just to draw payments.

The testimony rests on GAO report GAO-07-818, dated July 9, 2007. GAO told how far the department keeps to its own rules on estate payments. It set out the scale of payments made to dead people. Stronger controls are needed, GAO said, to stop bad payments before they leave the door.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1167t:
A disputed House race and its voting gear are under GAO review, as told in testimony GAO-07-1167T, dated August 3, 2007. In November 2006 about 18,000 undervotes were logged in Sarasota County, in Florida's 13th Congressional District race. An undervote means a ballot with no pick in that race. The result was contested in the House.

A House task force voted as one to seek GAO's aid. GAO set four aims: what systems were used, the scope of the undervote, tests run before the vote, and if more tests are needed. The statement is a status report. It tells what GAO has done, and what data it still studies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1247t:
New radiation portal monitors were meant to catch nuclear material at the border. GAO questioned how they were tested in GAO-07-1247T, issued September 18, 2007. The Domestic Nuclear Detection Office ran tests of the advanced spectroscopic portal monitors in early 2007. The tests took place at the Nevada Test Site. GAO checked the test methods and whether the results could support a production decision.

GAO found that the test methods were biased in the monitors' favor. The office ran early practice runs on nearly all test materials first. Vendors then tuned their machines to spot those same materials. GAO said such favorable conditions would not occur in real use. The tests also failed to probe the limits of detection. GAO urged the Secretary to delay certification until full testing was done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1257t:
A flu pandemic would not strike one place and end; it would roll on in waves. GAO assessed federal readiness in testimony GAO-07-1257T, presented September 26, 2007. The statement rests on GAO's report on the national Strategy and Plan for a pandemic. GAO judged both against its six traits of an effective national strategy. It also looked at who would lead the federal response.

GAO found that the Strategy and Plan fully met only one of the six traits. They defined the problem and its risks well. They did not cover resources, investments, and risk management at all. The Plan listed 324 action items with no ranking of which mattered most. Leadership roles were shared among many officials and still unclear in practice. GAO urged rigorous exercises to test those roles. It also urged a set time frame for updating the Plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-397t:
How the Pentagon sets the size of its ground forces is the focus of GAO testimony GAO-07-397T, delivered January 30, 2007. The Iraq war had strained the Army and Marine Corps. In its 2006 Quadrennial Defense Review, the Defense Department said active troop levels should stay flat. The Secretary of Defense then announced plans to add 92,000 troops.

Drawing on earlier GAO work, the testimony asks how the services study their needs. It checks whether those studies reflect new demands from the changed security setting. It also asks what proof the department gave Congress to back its requests. The statement warns that Congress should weigh the long-term cost of a larger force.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-427t:
Wildland fire costs keep rising with no joined plan to stop them, a point GAO drove home in testimony GAO-07-427T on January 30, 2007. Fires now burn far more acres than two decades ago. More homes sit in or near wildlands, which lifts both risk and cost. A century of fire suppression let dense brush build up, feeding worse blazes.

GAO summed up three reports plus an ongoing review. Federal agencies had no shared strategy that tied their steps together. Fuel clearing, cost sharing with states, and spending control each moved on their own track. A sound fuel plan might not arrive before 2009. GAO urged the agencies to set clear goals and one strategy, with costs named, so Congress can judge the trade-offs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-447t:
Children's health cover faces renewal, and GAO testimony GAO-07-447T, delivered February 1, 2007, sums up state experience. Congress built the State Children's Health Insurance Program (SCHIP) in August 1997. It targets low-income children whose families earn too much for Medicaid. Unlike Medicaid, the program caps federal funds. Congress set $40 billion for 1998 through 2007.

The testimony tracks enrollment trends and how state programs differ. It reviews how states spent their shares and what happened when funds ran short. States get 3 years to use each year's allotment. Leftovers shift to states that spent theirs. GAO drew on census data, state reports, and federal payment records. Lawmakers weighing renewal get a clear view of what the first decade showed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-497t:
Health costs squeeze every payer, and GAO testimony GAO-07-497T, presented February 15, 2007, lays out the squeeze. For years GAO has warned that federal finances face a hard future. Aging trends plus rising health costs drive the strain. Within a few decades, retirement and health promises will claim a growing share of federal funds. Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid sit at the center of that math.

The testimony splits the problem in two. Public payers face the sheer growth of entitlement rolls. All payers, public and private, face rising prices and more use of care. It then turns to how hard those costs are to tame. GAO refreshed its budget model with fresh census and Medicare data for the occasion. The message is fiscal: health spending is the hinge on which the long-term budget swings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-507t:
Building a welcome hall under the Capitol is the project tracked in GAO testimony GAO-07-507T, delivered February 16, 2007. The Capitol Visitor Center had hit fresh snags in its fire protection and security systems. The project team was still costing those changes. GAO told the House panel that a full grade of schedule and final cost was not yet possible.

The remarks rest on facts as of February 5, 2007, and on the Architect of the Capitol's December 2006 schedule. They recap building progress since the last hearing on November 15, 2006. They then turn to the expected cost at completion and the state of funding. GAO's stance is careful: report what is known, flag what is not, and wait for the team's own analysis before judging the end date. The update is one in a long series on the project.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-547t:
Proof of value leads GAO's budget plea in testimony GAO-07-547T, delivered March 16, 2007, in support of its fiscal year 2008 request. In fiscal year 2006, GAO's work yielded $51 billion in financial benefits. That is a return of $105 for each dollar Congress spent on the agency. GAO also logged 1,342 gains with no dollar tag, from better public service to changed laws.

The testimony thanks Congress for rescue funds that averted a staff furlough in fiscal year 2007. Even so, pay adjustments could not be backdated to January 7, 2007. The year's work ranged over border security, Iraq, Hurricane Katrina, and the tax gap. Health and pay issues for troops also featured. Client surveys rated the work highly. The request asks that the funding line match the workload Congress itself assigns.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-567t:
Doctor pay rules that punish all for the spending of some are probed in GAO testimony GAO-07-567T, presented March 6, 2007. Medicare's sustainable growth rate system ties fee updates to total spending targets. Spending has run past target for years. The formula thus calls for fee cuts. Since 2003, Congress or officials have blocked each cut, which only defers the bill.

A House health panel asked GAO for early findings on a new angle: practice patterns. Some doctors order far more care than peers for like patients. GAO reports how private buyers spot and press such outliers. It shares early work on how many Medicare doctors look inefficient. Tools to find them across the whole program get a review. The goal is reform that trims waste without cutting access for patients who need care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-587t:
Doctors who bill Medicare while dodging their taxes are the target of GAO testimony GAO-07-587T, presented March 20, 2007. Medicare paid a reported $330 billion in benefits in calendar year 2005. Part B physicians, health professionals, and suppliers took about 20 percent of that sum. Past GAO work had found federal contractors sitting on billions in unpaid taxes. Congress asked for the same lens on Medicare providers.

GAO matched health department payment data against Internal Revenue Service debt files. It measured how much Part B providers owe. Case work then named providers tied to abusive or possibly criminal conduct. The last strand grades efforts to bar tax debtors from joining Medicare and to seize their payments for the debt. Data limits at the health department narrowed the hunt, GAO notes. A fuller report on other provider types was due later that year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-607t:
The nation's own books still cannot earn a clean audit, and GAO testimony GAO-07-607T, delivered March 20, 2007, delivers that verdict. By law, GAO audits the consolidated financial statements of the U.S. government each year. The fiscal year 2006 set is the subject here. Leaders in Congress and the White House need sound books to steer programs and judge results.

The flaws roll on. Large chunks of assets, debts, and costs cannot be reported with full trust. The true cost of some programs stays hidden. Assets sit at risk from weak guards, and deals get logged wrong. Day-to-day choices thus rest on shaky sums. GAO pairs the audit result with a plea: steady gains in agency bookkeeping are the only road out. Until the books clean up, a full picture of what the government owns and owes stays out of reach.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-617t:
Small airports may gain little from a grant reshuffle, and GAO testimony GAO-07-617T, given March 28, 2007, gives early math. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) wants to fund its next air traffic system in new ways. Its plan rewrites the Airport Improvement Program, which grants build funds to the 3,400 airports in the national system. Congress asked GAO to update the funding picture.

The statement adds up what airports have received for building work. It sets that sum against what FAA and the airport industry say the work will cost. The gap is wide at small fields. The proposed new split does not close it, the early analysis finds. Big hubs can raise their own cash through fees and bonds. Small fields cannot. The testimony makes no recommendations; the underlying study was still live. It serves as a caution flag mid-debate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-637t:
Iraq's security ministries cannot yet pay and supply their own forces, and GAO testimony GAO-07-637T, delivered March 22, 2007, gives early proof. The United States has provided about $15.4 billion to build Iraqi military and police forces. The November 2005 victory strategy makes those forces the path to a stable Iraq. GAO's statement draws on prior reports plus fresh field work in Iraq and budget papers from three U.S. sources.

Two strands make up the brief. The first follows the money from both nations into the two ministries. The second lists the management strains: shaky spending of capital budgets, thin personnel systems, and weak logistics. The Defense Department expects Iraq to sustain its forces by 2008. GAO doubts the date, given the record. A U.S. transition command filed comments on the draft; its pushback is noted in the record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-687t:
Anthrax testing in postal buildings is the topic of GAO-07-687T, testimony from March 29, 2007. In the fall of 2001, letters laced with anthrax spores went to two senators and to news outlets. Postal sites in New Jersey, Washington, D.C., and other places were tainted. GAO reviewed how federal agencies checked those sites for anthrax. It asked how the tests were done and whether the methods were proven sound.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Postal Service led the work. They sampled spots where spores seemed most likely to gather. That method can confirm a known threat. It cannot prove a building is clean when tests find nothing. A random sampling plan would have given that proof. None of the steps, from taking samples to lab tests, had been validated for anthrax. GAO made no new recommendations in the statement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-727t:
Missile defense buying is weighed in GAO-07-727T, testimony dated April 11, 2007. The Missile Defense Agency planned to spend $49 billion over five years. It builds the Ballistic Missile Defense System in two-year blocks. Block 2006 aimed to guard against attacks from North Korea and the Middle East. Congress tells GAO to grade the work each year. This statement sums up GAO's March 2007 report on fiscal year 2006 progress.

GAO urged a knowledge-based path for each part of the system. It also urged clear rules for reporting counts, costs, and results. In March 2007, it told the Defense Department to set firm baselines. It said procurement funds should pay for fielded gear, not tests. The department balked at reporting part by part. It said it would look for other ways to open the books. GAO found the balance between speed and control still off.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-777t:
The national plan to teach money skills is graded in GAO-07-777T, testimony dated April 30, 2007. A 2003 law created the Financial Literacy and Education Commission. It joins federal agencies that run money education efforts. GAO's December 2006 report judged the group's progress. It checked the national strategy the group wrote. It also checked its website and hotline and its work with outside partners. This statement sums up that report.

The strategy lacked key parts, GAO found. It did not set clear ways to measure results or assign accountability. The website had not been tested for ease of use. No outside reviewer checked federal programs for overlap. Links with nonprofit and private groups needed growth. GAO made four recommendations to close those gaps. The commission has since taken steps on some of them. GAO said more progress is needed for an effective national effort.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-797t:
A rocket fuel chemical in water is the topic of GAO-07-797T, testimony from April 25, 2007. Perchlorate has been used for decades in missiles, rockets, fireworks, and explosives. It dissolves fast and travels through water with ease. It has turned up in ground and surface water across the country. Studies link it to thyroid harm and risks to unborn children. In 2005, the Environmental Protection Agency set a safe dose level. It is 24.5 parts per billion.

GAO's May 2005 report urged the agency to track detections and cleanups. The agency still disagrees with that call. It does not systematically track where the chemical is found. GAO compiled the known spread of contamination for this statement. It also reviewed studies of the health risks. Without tracking, GAO said, the public cannot know where the chemical sits. Communities near test and firing sites face the most concern.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-827t:
Help from other nations for the Iraq war is tallied in GAO-07-827T, testimony GAO gave on May 9, 2007. In March 2003, a U.S.-led force began operations in Iraq. At the start, 48 nations backed the effort in some form. Thirty-eight nations besides the United States sent troops. Donors met in Madrid in October 2003 to pledge rebuilding funds. GAO tracked how those pledges held up over time. It also tracked U.S. funds that support partner troops.

Troop pledges from partners shrank as the war went on. Many nations cut or ended their deployments. The United States has paid to move, feed, and equip some partner forces. Donor cash for rebuilding lagged the sums pledged in Madrid. GAO set the pledges beside the aid that truly arrived. The statement rests on unclassified records only. It gives Congress a clear view of the burden the coalition still shares.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-897t:
The Capitol Visitor Center gets a fresh status check in GAO-07-897T, testimony dated June 27, 2007. The Architect of the Capitol runs the long-running build. GAO last reported on it at an April 24, 2007 hearing. This statement covers work since then through June 27. It reports the expected cost at completion and the funding on hand. GAO read schedules and financial reports. It also walked the site and spoke with the build team.

Construction moved ahead in the two months covered. The Architect still projects a June 27, 2008 completion date. GAO kept its cost estimate at about $592 million. With risk allowance, the total tops $600 million. About $538.4 million has been approved for the work. Delays hit most near-critical paths, though the main path held. A further $20 million is sought for fiscal year 2008. More funds may be needed later for claims.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-997t:
Border Patrol training for a fast-growing force is the topic of GAO testimony dated June 19, 2007, numbered GAO-07-997T. In May 2006, the President called for 6,000 new agents by the end of December 2008. That goal meant a 48 percent rise in force size over 2 years. Such growth raised doubts about the basic training program's capacity.

The testimony rests on a recent GAO report on the program's content, quality, and cost. It weighs how far the program shows the marks of sound training. It also gives the cost to train one new agent and sets that cost beside peer programs. Plans to train agents more efficiently close the statement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1157t:
Cyber duties of the homeland security department are summed up in GAO testimony GAO-08-1157T, dated September 16, 2008. Recent attacks show how much harm strikes on computer systems can cause. Federal law makes the department the focal point for cyber security work. That role covers systems that support vital sectors of the economy.

Since 2005, GAO has tracked the department's progress in this role. The testimony gathers GAO's key reports and their advice. It also folds in two reports issued the same day. GAO finds that the department needs to better address its cyber responsibilities. The statement maps where federal coordination still falls short.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-177t:
Risks to U.S. ideas and brands abroad fill GAO testimony GAO-08-177T of October 18, 2007. Industries that rest on intellectual property made up over half of U.S. exports. They employed about 18 million Americans in 2006. Protection abroad varies widely, though. Some nations serve as havens for faked and pirated goods. Such goods can also endanger health and safety.

Eight federal agencies work to guard these rights. Two bodies coordinate their efforts. The testimony lays out the risks firms face, with China a prime case. It also reviews how the government runs and aligns its enforcement work at home.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-207t:
Shared medical records between two departments are tracked in GAO testimony GAO-08-207T, presented October 24, 2007. The veterans' and defense departments both treat many of the same people. Sharing health data helps them give sound care. Since 1998, the pair has chased records that computers can read and act on, such as drug allergy alerts.

GAO found that sharing keeps growing through short-term links between current systems. A full shared electronic record remains out of reach, though. Plans have shifted focus and dates again and again. Past GAO reviews blamed weak accountability and poor planning. The testimony sums up where the long effort stands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-227t:
A Capitol construction update is given in GAO testimony GAO-08-227T, dated November 14, 2007. The Capitol Visitor Center is being built under the Capitol grounds. The Architect of the Capitol leads the work with a private construction manager. GAO has tracked the project for Congress over many hearings. This update states its status as of October 31, 2007.

The testimony reports building progress since the prior hearing on September 25, 2007. It gives the expected cost when work ends. It also states how fully the project is funded. GAO drew on schedules, financial reports, and its own site visits. Talks with fire and police officials fed the review.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-277t:
Cleanup funds for uranium plants are revisited in GAO testimony GAO-08-277T, presented on November 15, 2007. Three Cold War enrichment plants sit near Oak Ridge, Paducah, and Portsmouth. All are stained with radioactive and hazardous waste. Cleanup will cost billions and may take decades. A 1992 law set up a fund for the work, fed by utility charges and federal funds.

The testimony rests on GAO's report from 2004. Back then, GAO told Congress to extend the fund to 2010. It told the Energy Department to retest the fund's strength before that date. It also sought cleanup plans for two plants. The statement reports where those steps stand.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-357t:
Major oil spills are the subject of GAO testimony GAO-08-357T, presented on December 18, 2007. Under federal law, a spill's owner or operator pays first, up to a set limit, and a federal trust fund covers costs when the spiller cannot pay. The statement builds on GAO's September 2007 report and adds updates on the recent San Francisco spill.

GAO estimated that 51 spills costing at least $1 million each occurred from 1990 to 2006. Spillers and the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund spent between $860 million and $1.1 billion on removal in that span. Spill costs turn on factors such as the oil type, place, and cleanup scale. In its earlier report, GAO had urged the Coast Guard to test whether liability limits should vary by vessel type and to adjust them for inflation every 3 years. The Department of Homeland Security generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-457t:
The Department of Homeland Security's build-out is graded in GAO testimony GAO-08-457T, presented on February 13, 2008. The department opened in March 2003 with counterterrorism missions of wide scope. GAO judged progress from March 2003 to July 2007 in both mission work and management.

Progress came in every area, but mission work moved faster than management. Open problems include contractor oversight, financial controls, a performance-based personnel system, technology management, and the balance between trade flow and border security. Deep issues cut across the effort: no full transformation strategy, weak strategic planning, and gaps in risk management and information sharing. GAO notes it has made roughly 900 recommendations to the department over time, some now carried out.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-497t:
GAO-08-497T, a GAO testimony presented on February 14, 2008, covers ground force readiness. About 931,000 Army and Marine Corps members deployed for overseas operations between 2001 and July 2007, including about 312,000 Guard and Reserve members. The Defense Department reported obligating about $492.2 billion on these operations through September 2007.

Long tours in Iraq and Afghanistan have worn down readiness, GAO reports. Tours grew longer and mobilizations more frequent to hold force levels. Gear was pulled from units at home and from stored stocks, leaving those units short. Training narrowed to counterinsurgency work, with little time for other missions. Navy and Air Force staff and contractors filled some ground roles. If the pace holds, rebuilding readiness while fighting will strain the force further.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-527t:
GAO covers patent examiner hiring in its testimony GAO-08-527T, presented on February 27, 2008. The Patent and Trademark Office grants patents that guard new ideas. Rising volume and harder cases have stretched review times and grown the backlog of unexamined applications.

The office sets hiring by budget and training room, not by the staff needed to shrink the backlog, so hiring alone will not clear it. Attrition eats the gains: from 2002 through 2006, one examiner left for nearly every two hired, and 70 percent of leavers had under 5 years in. Managers blame personal fit, but 67 percent of examiners cite production goals as a reason to leave. GAO urged a full check of the assumptions behind those goals. The office agreed to act.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-587t:
GAO's own reform bill is the subject of testimony GAO-08-587T, presented on March 13, 2008. H.R. 3268, the Government Accountability Office Act of 2007, would change how the agency hires, pays, and runs its staff. The statement also reports a workforce survey Congress had requested.

The survey, run by the Employee Advisory Council, asked staff outside the senior ranks about two sore points. One is the Band II restructuring of analyst jobs. The other is the Watson Wyatt market-based pay study used to set salary ranges. The council, chartered in January 2000, speaks for employee groups across the agency. The testimony uses the survey results to show where staff support the reforms and where concern runs deep.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-637t:
Sharing terror tips across agencies sounds simple, but no one had spelled out what success looks like. GAO-08-637T, testimony dated July 23, 2008, reviews the Information Sharing Environment, the federal push to link terror data. It also covers fusion centers and rules for handling sensitive papers that are not secret.

A plan from November 2006 guided early steps, and yearly reports listed goals and projects. Yet the plan never fixed the scope of the shared pool, who leads what, or how to tell if sharing got better. GAO asked the program manager to define goals, set measures, and state the federal role with state centers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-647t:
Nurse anesthetists give most anesthesia care in VA hospitals, and many are near retirement age. About 500 work for the Department of Veterans Affairs. GAO-08-647T, testimony dated April 9, 2008, sums up a December 2007 report on how hard it is for VA sites to hire and keep them.

Most site leaders told GAO they struggle to recruit these nurses. Empty posts vary by site and have hurt care at some sites. More losses loom in the next 5 years as staff retire or leave. Pay below local market rates is the main cause named. The testimony covers the pay survey tool sites can use to raise local rates.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-677t:
A new visitor center under the Capitol was nearly done in spring 2008. GAO-08-677T, testimony dated April 15, 2008, updates the cost and timing picture as of that day. The Architect of the Capitol still aimed to open the center in November 2008.

By cost, the job stood 99 percent complete. Fire alarm testing moved ahead, and a temp permit was hoped for by July 31, 2008. Risks stayed live: about 8,800 fix-list tasks remained, plus a steady flow of change orders. A late part for the smoke exhaust system could also slow testing. GAO flags what to watch in the final stretch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-687t:
Lead in tap water shocked Washington, D.C. in 2004 and forced a cleanup deal. GAO-08-687T, testimony dated April 15, 2008, reviews the city's water fixes and the strain facing water systems nationwide. Ageing pipes, growth, security, and new rules all demand cash.

A added chemical keeps lead below the federal limit in tests. The long fix, swapping out some 35,000 lead lines at a cost of about $400 million, is being rethought. The city can only swap the public half of each line. Of 14,260 lines swapped, owners joined in for just 2,128. Half swaps may even spike lead for a time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-707t:
Before a different panel, GAO again presented its fiscal year 2009 funding case in GAO-08-707T, testimony dated April 30, 2008. The ask is $545.5 million, up 7.5 percent. The statement stresses rising demand: study requests climbed 14 percent in fiscal year 2007 and kept climbing into 2008. Most House and Senate panels had asked GAO for work in the past 3 years.

Mandates packed into new laws topped 160 in one year, and bills in play by February 2008 held more than 600 more possible tasks. GAO says past work paid off, with $45.9 billion in money gains in fiscal year 2007 alone. Readers can compare this fuller demand picture with the shorter April budget statement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-717t:
Families can cut college costs through grants, loans, or tax breaks, but the tax route is tricky. GAO-08-717T, testimony dated May 1, 2008, sums up a 2005 report on how the two aid paths compare and how well filers use the tax breaks.

Grant aid tends to reach lower-income families, while tax breaks demand more work from filers. They must spot the right break, learn tangled rules, and do the math right. In one check of 2005 returns, 19 percent of eligible filers claimed no break at all and lost savings. GAO weighs whether a simpler aid system would serve families better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-737t:
About 1,300 Social Security field offices served some 42 million people in fiscal year 2007. Baby boomers now retire in waves, while office staff has shrunk. GAO-08-737T, testimony dated May 8, 2008, asks how offices cope and what the strain costs the public.

Offices largely kept up from fiscal years 2005 to 2007. Staff output rose 4.9 percent, work moved between offices, and more people were steered online. But some checks on who still qualifies were put off, which can let bad payments run. Waits grew, calls went unanswered more often, and staff report high stress and thin training time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-767t:
Medicare has long paid more than market price for wheelchairs, oxygen gear, and like supplies. A test in two places let suppliers bid for the work instead. GAO-08-767T, testimony dated May 6, 2008, weighs a wider bidding plan for the 44 million people on Medicare.

In the test, bidding saved Medicare $7.5 million and patients $1.9 million, with no clear loss of access. Winners were picked from 50 to 55 percent of bids. Extra checks on supplier quality and finances could also cut bad payments. GAO backs the savings path but warns that close watch is key as bidding spreads.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-847t:
Reliable books matter for a government facing long-term money strain. GAO-08-847T, testimony dated June 5, 2008, reports on the fiscal year 2007 federal financial statements. For the 11th straight year, GAO could not vouch for the full set of books.

Three blocks stand in the way: deep money problems at the Defense Department, tangled dealings between agencies that will not square, and a weak process for building the combined books. Gains are real too. Many agency audits have improved, and the 2007 Statement of Social Insurance won a clean verdict. A new plain-language summary report also debuted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-897t:
Guards watch about 9,000 federal buildings where over a million people work or visit. The Federal Protective Service runs that guard force on about $1 billion a year, with 1,100 staff and 15,000 hired guards. GAO-08-897T, testimony dated June 19, 2008, lists the strains on the service.

Staff fell about 20 percent from fiscal years 2004 through 2007. Patrols were cut in many places. One reviewer found a building safety report that described a large building where only a vacant lot stood. A shift to inspector-led teams and 150 new hires may not cure the gaps. GAO urges a staffing strategy and better success measures.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-907t:
Duty-free access to U.S. markets for poor countries is the subject of GAO-08-907T, June 2008 testimony on trade preference programs. Four programs, including the Generalized System of Preferences and the African Growth and Opportunity Act, cut tariffs for many goods from over 130 countries. Two faced partial or full expiry in 2008, and Congress was weighing renewal. The testimony draws on two recent GAO studies.

Preference imports grew from $20 billion in 1992 to $92 billion in 2006, most of it after 2000. GAO lays out three trade-offs: helping exporters versus shielding U.S. industries, which keeps farm goods and apparel largely out; extra benefits for some regions that the poorest countries elsewhere miss; and long renewals that spur investment versus short ones that keep leverage. GAO had urged the Trade Representative to review the programs jointly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-917t:
Energy use on Capitol Hill is the subject of GAO-08-917T, June 2008 testimony on the Architect of the Capitol. GAO reported in April 2007 that 96 percent of the complex's greenhouse gas emissions came from electricity use and fossil fuel burning at the Capitol Power Plant. That report urged energy audits and a schedule for doing them. This testimony checks the follow-through.

The Architect has ranked buildings for audits by energy use and begun the first ones, and a contractor is doing early audits of Senate office buildings. No schedule yet explains the ranking or states expected costs, which GAO says Congress needs for funding decisions. Energy-saving projects have gone ahead, but not as part of an overall emissions plan, so gains stay piecemeal.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-947t:
A new U.S. military command for Africa is taking shape, and GAO-08-947T, July 2008 testimony, gives early observations on its stand-up. Announced in February 2007, AFRICOM is meant to strengthen security ties with African nations, build partner capacity, and support peace efforts. It is designed to blend defense and civilian staff for a whole-of-government approach, a first for a combatant command.

The Defense Department has moved existing work, such as exercises and aid programs, toward the command, with most transfers due by October 1, 2008. Of 1,304 approved headquarters jobs, about 980 should be filled by then, plus 13 seats for other agencies. Interim headquarters sit in Stuttgart, Germany. Costs to build and run the command are not yet fully estimated, and the original concept met resistance at home and in Africa.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-97t:
About 18,000 Sarasota County ballots in November 2006 showed no vote for Congress, and testimony GAO-08-97T of October 2, 2007 asks whether the voting machines were at fault. The race was for Florida's 13th district, and the House asked GAO to study the county's touch-screen machines, made by Election Systems and Software.

GAO's count of the data found no single machine or trait that explains the gap. Past tests give some trust, GAO says, but not enough. It proposes three more tests: check the software in a sample of machines, test all the ways a voter can pick a name, and test a machine set off level on purpose. Even then, GAO notes, the tests give strong trust, not proof.
